sections.heading: 3.2.1. Action Space with Model Binding
sections.text: For each pending leaf node v v , the router selects one action: (4) a ⁡ ( v ) ∈ { IO , CoT , Decompose } . a(v)\in\{\textsf{IO},\ \textsf{CoT},\ \textsf{Decompose}\}. Each action is tied to a model scale and prompting style: IO uses a small model for direct answering, CoT uses a medium model with chain-of-thought prompting, and Decompose uses a large model to expand a subgraph and produce a branch summary. Macro-action semantics of Decompose . Decompose acts as a macro-action that expands the current node by proposing child subtasks and a branch summary, after which the children are routed and executed recursively. Since the resulting cost depends on downstream routing choices and the induced topology, RouteGoT estimates expansion cost online and applies a plan-guided fallback when needed (Section 3.5 ).

sections.heading: 3.4.2. Budget Predictor: Ordinal Difficulty Budget Prediction
sections.text: Exact token costs are noisy, especially when an action expands the graph. Instead of regressing costs directly, we predict a stable difficulty budget that approximates the minimum compute regime needed. Budget construction. For training, we define the required cost as c req ( u ) = min a : y a ​ ( u ) = 1 c a ( u ) c_{\text{req}}(u)=\min_{a:\ y_{a}(u)=1}c_{a}(u) , excluding all-fail cases. Using global thresholds B 25 B_{25} and B 75 B_{75} as the 25th and 75th percentiles of c req c_{\text{req}} , we assign a 3-budget label t ⁡ ( u ) ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } t(u)\in\{0,1,2\} : (11) t ⁡ ( u ) = { 0 , c req ​ ( u ) ≤ B 25 , 1 , B 25 < c req ​ ( u ) ≤ B 75 , 2 , c req ​ ( u ) > B 75 . t(u)=\begin{cases}0,&c_{\text{req}}(u)\leq B_{25},\\ 1,&B_{25} B_{75}.\end{cases} These labels map to per-node caps ( B 0 , B 1 , B 2 ) = ( B 25 , B 75 , + ∞ ) (B_{0},B_{1},B_{2})=(B_{25},B_{75},+\infty) , where the top is left unbounded so the feasible set is never empty. sections.heading: 3.5. Inference with Global Budget Scheduler
sections.text: To enforce a user budget B total B_{\text{total}} while still supporting multi-step reasoning, RouteGoT uses a Global Budget Scheduler that shapes graph growth based on the remaining budget. Synthesis reserve. We reserve B syn = max ⁡ ( B min , α syn ​ B total ) B_{\text{syn}}=\max(B_{\min},\alpha_{\text{syn}}B_{\text{total}}) tokens for final synthesis, where α syn \alpha_{\text{syn}} is a fixed fraction and B min B_{\min} is a minimum reserve. Let C acc C_{\text{acc}} denote the accumulated cost so far; the remaining expandable budget is B rem = B total − C acc − B syn B_{\text{rem}}=B_{\text{total}}-C_{\text{acc}}-B_{\text{syn}} . The scheduler stops expansion once B rem ≤ 0 B_{\text{rem}}\leq 0 . Complexity-conditioned depth constraints. We gate recursive decomposition using a node difficulty signal. A node is marked Hard if (i) t ^ ​ ( v ) = 2 \hat{t}(v)=2 , or (ii) p ^ Decompose ​ ( v ) \hat{p}_{\textsf{Decompose}}(v) exceeds the best non-expansion option by a margin; otherwise it is Simple . We allow deeper recursion only for Hard nodes, while Simple nodes are restricted to shallow execution to avoid unproductive recursion. Budget-regulated adaptive branching. When executing Decompose , the scheduler adapts the branching width K ⁡ ( v ) K(v) based on the remaining budget ratio ρ = B rem / B total \rho=B_{\text{rem}}/B_{\text{total}} , and penalizes width by depth and current node count so that exploration is broader early and more conservative as resources diminish. Plan-guided fallback mechanism. Even when the router selects Decompose , executing all generated subtasks can exceed the remaining budget. RouteGoT therefore uses an optimistic decomposition procedure: it first generates a plan (child subtasks) and then estimates the downstream execution cost. If the plan is predicted to violate the remaining budget, we trigger plan-guided fallback, reuse the plan as high-level context, and solve the current node locally via SolveWithPlan . This turns an over-budget expansion into a plan-and-solve step, preserving robustness while extracting value from the initial planning cost.

sections.heading: 4.1.2. Baselines
sections.text: We compare RouteGoT with two classes of baselines: standard reasoning paradigms and adaptive routing methods instantiated in our GoT-style executor. Standard Reasoning Paradigms. We include common inference methods as reference points for accuracy and cost. IO and CoT ( Wei et al., 2022 ) use standard zero-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting, respectively. For structured reasoning, we evaluate ToT ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , GoT ( Besta et al., 2024 ) , and AGoT ( Pandey et al., 2025 ) . The original GoT framework assumes task-specific, hand-crafted graph schemas, which is difficult to scale to diverse, open-ended QA benchmarks. We therefore implement a generalized GoT variant that uses the same dynamic graph expansion logic as our framework, while forcing planning, execution, and synthesis to be carried out by the Large model. This variant avoids per-task schema design and acts as a schema-free upper bound that favors accuracy over cost. Adaptive Routing Baselines. To isolate the effect of routing, we keep the reasoning backbone and graph operations fixed and replace only the router with existing strategies. All routers use the same text embeddings and are trained (or indexed) on the same Router Training Data (Sec. 4.1.1 ). The Random Router samples actions uniformly; we report the mean over 10 runs. The KNN-Router retrieves the k = 10 k=10 nearest training instances by embedding similarity and selects the expert with the best estimated score. For learning-based routers, we adapt three representative methods. EmbedLLM ( Zhuang et al., 2025 ) selects the expert with the highest predicted success probability and does not model cost. Route-to-Reason (RTR) ( Pan et al., 2025 ) predicts both success probability and token cost and chooses the expert that maximizes a utility objective. RouteLLM ( Ong et al., 2025 ) is a binary router for strong/weak model selection, and we adapt it to choose between our cheapest and most expensive strategies by training separate checkpoints for different cost and performance trade-offs.

sections.heading: 4.1.3. Implementation Details
sections.text: We summarize the key configuration choices for our experimental framework. Full hyperparameters, hardware details, and baseline-specific settings are in Appendix C . Backbone Models and Strategy Binding. We use the Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) family to instantiate actions with different capability and cost profiles. Concretely, the Small (4B) model runs Direct for simple IO prompting, the Medium (8B) model runs CoT for multi-step reasoning, and the Large (30B) model runs Decompose for planning and graph expansion. The learned components in RouteGoT use lightweight 0.6B adapters to keep routing overhead small. Unified Graph Environment. All graph-based methods, including baselines, run in the same GoT-style executor to ensure comparability. To reflect resource-limited settings, we cap the maximum graph depth at 3 and the branch at 5. We run all experiments with the vLLM inference engine on 4 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Router and Baseline Setup. All learning-based routers share the same sentence encoder for node inputs, using all-mpnet-base-v2 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 . For cost-aware baselines (KNN, RTR, and RouteLLM), we report three operating points (Performance, Balanced, and Cost-Saving) obtained by varying the cost penalty coefficient β \beta . Unless stated otherwise, we use the Balanced setting in the main comparisons.

sections.heading: 4.2. Performance and Efficiency Analysis (RQ1)
sections.text: Table 2 and Table 3 present the performance of RouteGoT across seven benchmarks. For brevity, we report average output tokens in Table 2 , with input tokens provided in Table 5 . RouteGoT exhibits a favorable balance between reasoning accuracy and computational efficiency, reaching or sharing the top performance across all evaluated tasks. Compared to structured baselines such as AGoT, RouteGoT provides an average accuracy gain of 8.1 percentage points while reducing output token consumption by 79.1%. The high cost associated with AGoT is primarily attributed to repeated graph executions involving extensive context concatenation and lengthy prompts, leading to substantial input token overhead on certain datasets. These efficiency gains remain consistent across diverse tasks; for example, on HotpotQA, accuracy increases from 72.0% to 88.0% alongside a 77.1% reduction in output tokens. This decrease in token volume corresponds to lower inference latency, as RouteGoT consistently outperforms AGoT in speed and achieves nearly a 6 × 6\times speedup over GoT* on MoreHopQA. Adaptive routing baselines like RTR often sacrifice solution quality for speed, whereas RouteGoT maintains high accuracy on complex reasoning tasks. While RTR achieves low latency, RouteGoT exceeds its performance by an average of 9.8 points with comparable token usage. On HybridQA, RouteGoT improves accuracy to 91.0% from the 68.0% achieved by RTR. Furthermore, on search-intensive tasks such as Crosswords, RouteGoT is both more accurate and faster than RTR, requiring 37.09s compared to 47.00s. These results suggest that rather than pruning indiscriminately to meet budget constraints, RouteGoT strategically allocates computational resources to critical nodes, thereby avoiding the performance degradation typical of aggressive cost-reduction strategies. sections.heading: 4.3. Budget Controllability and Stability (RQ2)
sections.text: Figure 3 shows how accuracy changes as we vary the per-question compute budget. We sweep a global token cap B total B_{\text{total}} , enforced on total tokens across all model calls. RouteGoT remains reliable under tight constraints. At the lowest budget, it reaches 54.3% accuracy, exceeding AGoT by 16.4 points and RTR by 10.9 points. This pattern suggests that in-graph routing can still prioritize the most useful expansions when budget limits sharply restrict search. Several structured baselines show a clear cold-start behavior: under small budgets, ToT, GoT*, and CoT fall below the 4-way random-guessing level (25%) and only become competitive after the budget increases. As B total B_{\text{total}} grows, RouteGoT improves steadily, tracks the best curve across the sweep, and peaks at 65.7%. Its performance declines gradually as budgets tighten, with an 11.4-point gap between the strictest and most lenient settings. By comparison, AGoT is more budget-sensitive, varying by about 20 points, and CoT, GoT*, and ToT need substantially larger budgets to approach their best operating regions. Even at the highest budget, RouteGoT keeps an advantage of about 7 points over AGoT. Taken together, the results indicate that budget-aware scheduling and node-level routing support both low-budget robustness and a higher accuracy ceiling under practical constraints. A practical factor is that graph-based methods pay noticeable input overhead from repeated context injection and multi-call prompts. When B total B_{\text{total}} limits total tokens, this overhead tightens the effective budget more than output-token counts alone would imply, especially for methods with heavier prompting such as AGoT. RouteGoT reduces this cost by using compact branch summaries and lightweight routing, leaving more of the budget for the reasoning steps that most affect the final prediction.

sections.heading: 4.6. Ablation Study
sections.text: We study the role of each learned component in RouteGoT with ablations on HotpotQA, MoreHopQA, and HybridQA. We compare the full system with two variants. The w/o Budget Predictor (BP) variant replaces the ordinal Budget Predictor with a continuous cost regressor, testing whether coarse, discrete budgets provide a more reliable signal than direct cost regression. The w/o BP + PolicyNet (PN) variant further removes PolicyNet and selects actions using Success Predictor scores, which tests whether learned decision rules are necessary beyond confidence-based routing. Table 4. Comparison of RouteGoT against variants with ablated components. Method HotpotQA MoreHopQA HybridQA Acc (%) Tokens Acc (%) Tokens Acc (%) Tokens RouteGoT 88.0 592 77.0 665 91.0 700 w/o BP 86.0 2438 78.0 2649 89.0 1634 w/o BP + PN 78.0 2020 70.0 2951 83.0 1722 Analysis. Table 4 reports the results. Replacing the Tier Predictor with a continuous regressor (w/o BP) consistently increases token use, nearly quadrupling cost on HotpotQA (592 vs. 2438) and similarly inflating MoreHopQA. Accuracy stays close, but largely because the router spends more tokens, so efficiency drops sharply. This supports the use of ordinal tiers as a stable mechanism for enforcing per-node budgets, rather than relying on noisy point estimates that drift toward expensive choices. Removing PolicyNet as well (w/o BP+PN) reduces accuracy substantially, with HotpotQA falling from 88.0% to 78.0%. This suggests that confidence scores alone are not enough to choose effective graph actions, especially when deciding whether to expand a subgraph. PolicyNet provides the missing coupling between success signals, budget constraints, and action selection that improves the overall cost accuracy balance.
